title: Phrasal verbs, dependent prepositions and idioms
tagline: Multi-meaning phrasal verbs, what particles mean, and the dependent prepositions that go with them.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (dependent prepositions and particles)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (PUT, INTO, OFF, DOWN, OUT, OF, UP)
Listening Parts 1 and 3 — recognising phrasal verbs at natural speed
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — sounding idiomatic instead of translating word for word
why: Phrasal verbs and dependent prepositions are the clearest giveaway of a non-native answer in Part 2 and Part 4: the grammar is often right, but the small word is wrong. At C1, examiners also expect range — using put up with instead of always reaching for tolerate — because idiomatic phrasal verbs are how fluent speakers actually talk, not just formal alternatives learned for an exam.

rows.label: Object position
cells: always after the whole phrasal verb

rows.label: With a pronoun
cells: must go between verb and particle

rows.label: Common error
cells: turn down it (wrong with a pronoun)

diagrams.title: From a single verb to a phrasal verb

before.text: I can no longer tolerate his constant excuses.

after.text: I can no longer put up with his constant excuses.

steps: Replace the single verb (tolerate) with the three-part phrasal verb.
Put up with is always inseparable: the object goes after with.
This kind of phrasal verb sounds more natural in speech and semi-formal writing than its single-word equivalent.

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: same verb + particle, different meaning by context
Please use up the leftover paint before we buy more.
verb + out = vanish or come to light
The tradition slowly died out after the schools merged.
verb + off = cancel, separate or interrupt
The final was called off because of the storm.
verb + through = get to the end of something hard
It took hours to get through the reading list.
verb + object + particle, or verb + particle + object
The committee will look into the complaint.
She's capable of far more than she thinks.

examples.text: Can you turn down the music? He also decided to turn down the scholarship.
examples.note: turn down: reduce volume, or refuse an offer

examples.text: Miss Vega will go over the essay plan before we start, then we'll go over the bridge on the way home.
examples.note: go over: review, or physically cross

examples.text: The team needs to pick up the pace, and someone still has to pick up the trophy from the office.
examples.note: pick up: increase, or collect something

examples.text: Use up the paint before we buy more; don't waste it.
The old custom slowly died out once the school merged with another.
examples.note: out = disappearance, coming to an end

examples.text: The match was called off because of the storm.
Turn the offer down, or turn it down — both work; only turn down it is wrong.
examples.note: separable: object can go before or after the particle, but a pronoun must go between

examples.text: The council will look into the complaint as soon as possible.
examples.note: inseparable: the object always follows the whole phrase

examples.text: You can always rely on Nadia to stay calm under pressure.
examples.note: inseparable, verb + dependent preposition already built in

examples.text: She has always been capable of far more than her grades suggest.
The committee finally agreed on a date for the trip.
After weeks of arguing, they decided to put up with the situation instead of fighting it.
examples.note: three-part phrasal verb, idiomatic, means tolerate

watch_out.wrong: Please turn down it, it's too loud.
watch_out.why: with a pronoun, separable phrasal verbs must split: verb + pronoun + particle.

watch_out.wrong: The council will look the complaint into.
watch_out.right: The council will look into the complaint.
watch_out.why: look into is inseparable; the object always comes after the whole phrase.

watch_out.wrong: She's capable to do far more than she thinks.
watch_out.right: She's capable of doing far more than she thinks.
watch_out.why: capable takes the dependent preposition of, followed by a gerund, not a to-infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: I can't put up his constant excuses any more.
watch_out.right: I can't put up with his constant excuses any more.
watch_out.why: put up with is a fixed three-part phrasal verb; with cannot be dropped.

watch_out.wrong: The tradition died off after the merger.
watch_out.right: The tradition died out after the merger.
watch_out.why: die out (disappear gradually), not die off, is the fixed phrasal verb for a custom or species disappearing.

watch_out.wrong: We agreed with a date for the trip.
watch_out.right: We agreed on a date for the trip.
watch_out.why: agree on/about a decision; agree with is for agreeing with a person or opinion.

dialogue.title: Planning the Arequipa trip
dialogue.context: Miss Vega and the students sort out the details of the Arequipa trip after the museum on the itinerary suddenly closes for renovation.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, let's go over the plan for the Arequipa trip.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Can we turn down the idea of the six a.m. bus? Nobody will survive that.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Agreed. Let's look into a later departure instead.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Also, the museum visit got called off — it's closed for renovation.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: That's a shame — I was really looking forward to that.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: We'll come up with an alternative. Any ideas?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: The old chocolate museum, maybe? Local traditions there haven't died out yet.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I can put up with a longer walk if the museum's worth it.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Fine by me. Someone needs to sort out the tickets before Friday, though.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I'll take care of that — I'm capable of more than just complaining.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Perfect. Let's wrap up here and confirm everything by email.

practice.instructions: Choose the correct phrasal verb or expression.

items.sentence: Could you ___ the music a bit? It's too loud for studying.
items.why: turn down = reduce the volume or intensity of something.

items.sentence: The council promised to ___ the noise complaints properly.
items.why: look into = investigate; look at and look for don't fit a formal promise to investigate complaints.

items.sentence: The concert was ___ because of the storm warning.
items.why: called off = cancelled; called out and called up mean something different (summoned, drafted).

items.sentence: That old custom has almost completely ___ in the city.
items.why: died out = gradually disappeared, typically of a custom, species or tradition.

items.sentence: I really can't ___ his constant complaining any longer.
items.why: put up with = tolerate; the particle order in put down with / put off with doesn't exist.

items.sentence: She's perfectly ___ organising the whole event herself.
items.why: capable takes the dependent preposition of, followed by a gerund (organising).

items.sentence: We finally ___ a solution everyone could accept.
items.why: came up with = thought of or produced (an idea or solution).

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the missing particle or preposition.

items.sentence: Could you turn ___ the music? It's too loud.
The council promised to look ___ the complaints properly.
The final was called ___ because of the storm.
The custom slowly died ___ after the two schools merged.
I can't put up ___ his constant excuses any longer.
She's perfectly capable ___ organising the whole trip herself.
We finally came ___ with a solution everyone could accept.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: I can no longer tolerate his constant excuses.
The council will investigate the noise complaints.
The concert was cancelled because of the storm warning.
Please could you reduce the volume of the music?
The tradition gradually disappeared after the merger.
She is fully able to organise the whole event by herself.
items.second_end: organising the whole event by herself.

items.first: They eventually thought of a solution everyone could accept.

summary: Many phrasal verbs change meaning completely with context: turn down the volume, or turn down an offer.
Particles carry meaning of their own: up = completion, out = disappearance, off = separation, through = getting past a difficulty.
Separable phrasal verbs split with a pronoun (turn it down); inseparable ones never split (look into it).
Dependent prepositions are fixed and must be learned with the word: capable of, agree on, rely on.
Idiomatic phrasal verbs like put up with and come up with sound far more natural at C1 than their single-word equivalents.
